newsitem.title: UK: British insurer hikes direct motor rates.
newsitem.headline: British insurer hikes direct motor rates.

text.p: A leading British direct motor insurer said on Thursday it has over recent weeks dramatically increased the prices it charges customers for motor cover.
But in a saturated market, which at best is only just coming out of a deep pricing trough, and where competition remains fierce, big industry-wide price rises may still be some way off.

Ray Pierce, managing director of Guardian Direct, the direct selling personal motor insurance arm of British composite Guardian Royal Exchange Plc, told Reuters he believes the last few months have seen a sustained rise in personal motor premium rates across much of the direct sales sector.

He said that Guardian Direct, which has 650,000 customers or about three percent of the entire British motor insurance market and which in April bought RAC (Royal Automobile Club) Insurance Brokers, has increased base premium rates for personal motor insurance policies by more than 10 percent since June.
Retentions were holding at over eighty percent, he added.

Guardian said when it released interim results in July that it had put through selective price increases of up to five percent on motor policies and expected to see rises of up to seven percent in direct motor rates over the course of the next year.
"Everybody in the direct market is now on average pushing up their prices," said Pierce in a telephone interview. "There has been an increase in the latter part of the year."
Guardian's biggest rival, Royal Bank of Scotland's Direct Line Insurance, which sells more motor policies than any insurer in Britain, said the price rises were not unexpected.
But Direct Line added that it has not put through baseline increases of anything approaching the 10 percent level and many industry analysts still remain sceptical of a widespread upturn.

"We are not surprised. We have said for a long time the pricing in the market was unsustainable and that price rises, consolidation and withdrawals were inevitable," said chief executive Ian Chippendale.
"We are making small selective increases but we suggest that over the next 18 months those increases are not going to amount to more than two to three percent," added spokesman Adrian Webb.
"The overall state of motor premium rates in the industry is that people are losing money," he said.

Intense competition in Britain's overcrowded insurance sector has pushed personal motor premiums down by around 20 percent over the last two years. Several insurers have this year provided evidence of a very modest and selective rebound, but it remains to be seen how sustained or far reaching this will be.

Industry analysts who attended a briefing on Wednesday at Guardian Direct's offices in Colchester were also told of the significant rise in the insurer's base rates, and given the company's interpretation of how competitors are pricing.

Guardian told the analysts that a sampling of prices in the direct market showed that in September, 87 percent of prices had changed and 67 percent of those had increased. In October, the corresponding figures were 64 percent and 60 percent.

The direct motor market is the frontline of industry pricing. There is no intermediary between insurer and customer, so the information flow is cleaner, which means the insurer can react quickly to changing market conditions.
"When we did this research last year, we were really seeing more prices falling than rising," said Pierce.

But many analysts are sceptical of a turnaround for the direct market in the short term. BZW analyst Hugh Pye this week cut his forecast for Direct Line's profits for 1996 to 16 million pounds from 50 million and recommended selling shares in Royal Bank of Scotland.
Guardian shares ended five pence up at 272-1/2p.
